Connecting a data source

This guide covers choosing and configuring a source connector — the first step of any new pipeline.

Choosing a connector type

You haveUse
A relational database you can grant replication access toPostgres
Files landing in object storageAmazon S3
An existing event streamKafka
A third party that can push to a URL you controlWebhook

Authenticating

Each connector type has its own credential shape — see the Connectors endpoint for the full parameter list per type.

{{ds:component/alert|variant=warning|title=Least-privilege credentials|body_html=

Grant the connector only the access it needs — read-only replication for Postgres sources, a scoped IAM role for S3, never a superuser or admin credential.

}}

Verifying the connection

A newly created connector reports health: degraded until its first successful read or write, then flips to healthy. If it goes straight to down, double check credentials before opening a support ticket.

Error handling & recovery

Every event that fails a transform or a destination write is retried automatically. This guide covers how that works and what to do when retries run out.

Automatic retries

Failed events retry with exponential backoff — 1s, 2s, 4s, up to a per-pipeline configurable ceiling. Most transient failures (a destination hiccup, a rate-limited third party) resolve within the first few attempts.

{{ds:component/code-block|filename=pipeline-retry-config.json|language=json|code={ "retry_policy": { "max_attempts": 5, "backoff": "exponential", "initial_delay_ms": 1000 } }}}

Dead-lettering

An event that exhausts its retries is moved to that pipeline's dead-letter queue rather than dropped silently.

{{ds:component/alert|variant=danger|title=Dead-lettered events don't retry themselves|body_html=

Once in the dead-letter queue, an event stays there until you replay it or explicitly discard it — it will not retry again on its own.

}}

Replaying events

Use the Events endpoint's replay action to re-run a specific dead-lettered event once the underlying issue is fixed.

{{ds:component/code-block|filename=replay.sh|language=bash|code=curl -X POST https://api.godzilladocs.dev/v3/events/evt_8f2c1a90/replay \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $GODZILLA_API_KEY"}}

Watching for failures

Subscribe to pipeline.failed via Webhooks so you find out about dead-lettered events before a customer does. See also Monitoring & alerts.

Scheduling & triggers

A pipeline runs either on a schedule or in response to incoming events. This guide covers both.

Scheduled pipelines

Set a schedule (a cron expression) when creating or updating a pipeline via the Pipelines endpoint. Godzilla runs the pipeline once per schedule tick, processing whatever new data is available from the source since the last run.

{{ds:component/code-block|filename=schedule.json|language=json|code={ \"schedule\": \"0 */4 * * *\" }}}

Event-triggered pipelines

Omit schedule and the pipeline instead runs continuously, processing events as its source connector emits them — the right choice for sources like Kafka or a Webhook connector where near-real-time matters.

{{ds:component/alert|variant=info|title=Choosing between them|body_html=

Use a schedule for sources that batch naturally (a nightly file drop to S3). Use event-triggered for anything where minutes matter.

}}

Pausing and resuming

A paused pipeline skips scheduled ticks entirely and buffers nothing for event-triggered sources — resuming picks up new events going forward, not a backlog. To reprocess a time range instead, see the replay flow in Error handling & recovery.

{{ds:component/docs-pagination|prev_href={{cms:item/c484e924-5ec5-4c95-81ad-c8c31b702a7f}}|prev_label=Error handling & recovery|next_href={{cms:item/522ba05b-8a21-43dd-82ac-ece908ce14b4}}|next_label=Monitoring & alerts}}", "version_token": "48663fb1-36e6-41b3-90ba-083793406827", "created_at": "2026-08-22T00:46:57.463Z", "updated_at": "2026-08-22T00:47:41.321Z", "placement_id": "8ed279da-c9eb-46e0-bd2f-4f15df9f1c76", "folder_id": "c3e0ba4a-a491-4265-9848-556d298e6b6b", "file_name": "scheduling-and-triggers" } }

Quotas & billing {{ds:component/chip|label=v2|variant=primary}} {{ds:component/chip|label=Stable|variant=success}}

Godzilla accounts operate under usage quotas determined by your plan tier. Quotas apply at the workspace level across API request throughput, monthly event volume, and concurrent pipeline resources.

Plan tiers

Each workspace is assigned to a tier that dictates default rate limits and monthly event capacities.

Plan Rate limit Monthly events Active pipelines Support SLA
Starter 100 req / min 50,000 3 Community
Standard 1,000 req / min 1,000,000 25 1 business day
Enterprise Custom (10,000+ req / min) Custom / Unlimited Unlimited 24/7 dedicated SLA

What happens when you exceed a quota

Exceeding limits is handled differently depending on whether you exceed a per-minute API request rate or a monthly event volume quota.

API rate limits (HTTP 429)

If your application sends more requests in a one-minute window than your tier allows, the API returns a 429 Too Many Requests status code. Responses include a Retry-After header indicating how many seconds to wait before resuming requests. See Rate limits for header details and retry strategies.

Monthly event quotas

Monthly event usage resets on the first day of your billing cycle. When approaching or exceeding event limits:

  • 80% and 100% threshold alerts: Account admins receive email notifications and webhook lifecycle events (workspace.quota_warning) when approaching your limit.
  • Standard plan overages: On the Standard tier, pipelines continue running without interruption. Overage events are billed at $0.15 per 10,000 events on your next invoice.
  • Starter plan cap: Starter tier workspaces pause pipeline ingestion once the 50,000 event limit is reached until the next billing cycle or an upgrade to Standard.

Resource limits (pipelines and connectors)

If you attempt to create more active pipelines or connectors than your plan allows, the API returns a 403 Forbidden with code quota_exceeded.

Upgrading and quota increases

You can upgrade your plan or add billing details directly from workspace settings. If your workload requires higher burst rate limits or tailored enterprise terms, reach out via Troubleshooting / FAQ.

{{ds:component/alert|variant=info|title=Monitoring usage|body_html=

Check your current monthly event consumption and active pipeline counts anytime in the workspace dashboard or via the workspace metadata endpoint.

Godzilla is built from core concepts that compose into everything else in these docs. Understanding how they relate makes the rest of the platform — guides, API reference, SDKs — much easier to follow.

{{ds:component/card|href={{cms:item/0881cc13-706b-45dc-b215-08b706dc8fdb}}|tag=Concept|title=Pipelines|description=Named, versioned workflows that move data from a source to a destination through optional transforms.}} {{ds:component/card|href={{cms:item/3cc1aa67-f674-447d-8dda-ac55a42c26eb}}|tag=Concept|title=Connectors|description=Pre-built integrations to external systems — sources, destinations, or both.}} {{ds:component/card|href={{cms:item/aaba4e33-be69-4693-8066-1c2f622b674b}}|tag=Concept|title=Events|description=The atomic unit of data flowing through a pipeline, plus the platform's own lifecycle events.}} {{ds:component/card|href={{cms:item/88ecedb3-543b-4dcf-b985-6fb94e4eaa95}}|tag=Concept|title=Schemas|description=Declarative contracts that define and validate the structure of event payloads flowing through pipelines.}}

How they fit together

A pipeline reads events from a source connector, validates their schemas, transforms them, and writes them to a destination connector. Everything else in Godzilla — retries, webhooks, monitoring — is built on top of that single loop.

Definitions

Short definitions for every term used throughout these docs.

Pipeline
A named, versioned workflow that moves data from a source connector, through optional transforms, to a destination connector.
Connector
A pre-built integration to an external system — a source, a destination, or both.
Event
The atomic unit of data moving through a pipeline, or a platform lifecycle notification like pipeline.failed.
Schema
A declarative contract specifying the structure, types, and validation rules for event payloads.
Webhook
An outbound HTTP request Godzilla sends to a URL you control when a subscribed event occurs.
Dead-letter queue
Where an event goes after exhausting its retries, rather than being dropped. See Error handling & recovery.
Cursor pagination
The pagination style used by every v2 list endpoint. See Rate limits.
Quota
Usage allowances assigned to a workspace based on its plan tier, covering request throughput and monthly event volume. See Quotas & billing.
Workspace
The top-level account boundary an API key is scoped to.

args.short_description: Reshape, filter, and enrich events as they pass through a pipeline.
args.body:
Transforming events in flight

Transforms are intermediate processing steps applied to events as they travel between a source connector and a destination in a pipeline. You can use transforms to reshape payload structures, filter out unwanted records, and enrich events with additional context.

1. Reshaping events

Use reshape transforms to rename fields, restructure nested objects, or strip sensitive and unneeded keys before writing to downstream storage.

{{ds:component/code-block|filename=reshape-transform.json|language=json|code={ \"type\": \"reshape\", \"config\": { \"rename\": { \"customer_email\": \"email\", \"amt_cents\": \"amount_cents\" }, \"drop\": [\"internal_notes\", \"raw_ip\"] } }}}

2. Filtering events

Filtering lets you conditionally route or drop events based on payload criteria. Non-matching events are discarded immediately, saving destination throughput and storage.

{{ds:component/code-block|filename=filter-transform.json|language=json|code={ \"type\": \"filter\", \"config\": { \"condition\": \"payload.status == 'completed' && payload.amount_cents > 0\" } }}} {{ds:component/alert|variant=info|title=Dropped events|body_html=

Filtered-out events do not trigger retries or dead-letter queue entries; they are treated as successfully skipped.

}}

3. Enriching events

Enrichment transforms add metadata, computed values, or static contextual fields to the event payload before delivery.

{{ds:component/code-block|filename=enrich-transform.json|language=json|code={ \"type\": \"enrich\", \"config\": { \"add_fields\": { \"environment\": \"production\", \"processed_by\": \"godzilla-pipeline-v2\" } } }}}

Configuring transforms in a pipeline

Transforms are supplied as an ordered array on the pipeline definition. Godzilla executes each transform sequentially for every event.

{{ds:component/code-block|filename=pipeline-with-transforms.json|language=json|code={ \"name\": \"orders-with-transforms\", \"source_connector_id\": \"conn_pg_orders\", \"destination_connector_id\": \"conn_snowflake_dw\", \"transforms\": [ { \"type\": \"filter\", \"config\": { \"condition\": \"payload.amount_cents > 0\" } }, { \"type\": \"reshape\", \"config\": { \"drop\": [\"raw_ip\"] } }, { \"type\": \"enrich\", \"config\": { \"add_fields\": { \"region\": \"us-east\" } } } ] }}} {{ds:component/alert|variant=warning|title=Order of execution matters|body_html=

Because transforms run sequentially, placing filter steps first avoids unnecessary processing on events that will ultimately be dropped.

}}

Next steps

Learn how Godzilla deals with transformation and destination write failures in Error handling & recovery, configure steps via the Transforms endpoint, or manage your pipelines directly using the Pipelines endpoint.

Building your first pipeline

This guide walks through creating a pipeline end to end: a source connector, a destination connector, and the pipeline that ties them together.

{{ds:component/alert|variant=info|title=Before you start|body_html=

You'll need an API key. See Authentication in Getting Started if you don't have one yet.

}}

1. Create a source connector

We'll pull orders from Postgres. See Connectors for the full catalog of types.

{{ds:component/code-block|filename=create-source.sh|language=bash|code=curl -X POST https://api.godzilladocs.dev/v2/connectors \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $GODZILLA_API_KEY" \ -d '{\"type\":\"postgres\",\"direction\":\"source\",\"config\":{\"connection_string\":\"postgres://...\"}}'}} {{ds:component/code-block|filename=create_source.go|language=go|code=source, err := client.Connectors.Create(ctx, godzilla.ConnectorParams{ Type: \"postgres\", Direction: \"source\", Config: map[string]string{ \"connection_string\": \"postgres://...\", }, })}}

2. Create a destination connector

We'll write to Snowflake.

args.body:
Error handling & recovery

Every event that fails a transform or a destination write is retried automatically. This guide covers how that works and what to do when retries run out.

Automatic retries

Failed events retry with exponential backoff — 1s, 2s, 4s, up to a per-pipeline configurable ceiling. Most transient failures (a destination hiccup, a rate-limited third party) resolve within the first few attempts.

{{ds:component/code-block|filename=pipeline-retry-config.json|language=json|code={ "retry_policy": { "max_attempts": 5, "backoff": "exponential", "initial_delay_ms": 1000 } }}}

Dead-lettering

An event that exhausts its retries is moved to that pipeline's dead-letter queue rather than dropped silently.

{{ds:component/alert|variant=danger|title=Dead-lettered events don't retry themselves|body_html=

Once in the dead-letter queue, an event stays there until you replay it or explicitly discard it — it will not retry again on its own.

}}

Replaying events

Use the Events endpoint's replay action to re-run a specific dead-lettered event once the underlying issue is fixed.

{{ds:component/code-block|filename=replay.sh|language=bash|code=curl -X POST https://api.godzilladocs.dev/v3/events/evt_8f2c1a90/replay \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $GODZILLA_API_KEY"}}

Watching for failures

Subscribe to pipeline.failed via Webhooks so you find out about dead-lettered events before a customer does. See also Monitoring & alerts.
